comment: I am writing to express my sincere support for the development of affordable housing in our beautiful city of Park City, Utah. As an employee and active member of the community, I strongly believe that providing affordable housing opportunities is crucial for the well-being and prosperity of our diverse population. The lack of affordable housing options has created a growing disparity, limiting the accessibility and inclusivity that are the cornerstones of a thriving community. By prioritizing the development of affordable housing, we have the opportunity to foster a more inclusive, diverse, and resilient Park City. Affordable housing not only benefits low-income individuals and families, but it also enhances the overall social fabric and economic vitality of our city.Affordable housing enables individuals from different socio-economic backgrounds to live closer to their places of employment. This is particularly vital for the workers who contribute to the success of our local businesses, including service industry employees, healthcare professionals, educators, and public servants. By ensuring their ability to live in the community they serve, we can retain a diverse and talented workforce. We can bring people from different backgrounds together, fostering a stronger sense of community and promoting social cohesion. When individuals and families can afford to live and work in Park City, they have more disposable income to spend locally, supporting our businesses and bolstering our economy. Affordable housing preserves the diverse character and unique spirit of our city, making it an attractive destination for visitors and residents alike.I understand that developing affordable housing can present challenges, including financial considerations and finding suitable locations. However, I believe that with thoughtful planning, community engagement, and collaboration, we can overcome these hurdles and create a more equitable Park City.

comment: Good morning. I'm following up with a written version of the comments I offered at the December 5th meeting in order that they become part of the written public record. Thank you. Angela Moschetta Old Town Resident It is widely understood in this building and this community that Planning Commission doesn’t negotiate. An applicant brings forth an application for development. If the applicant seeks exceptions to the code, impacts are mitigated through over amended proposals and subsequent meetings. The burden is on the applicant to bring forth a compliant and/or reasonable application and then eventually be subject to a vote. Last year, someone in this building decided that Planning Commission should look at only the circulation and traffic aspects of Deer Valley’s MPD and, when able to forward a positive recommendation on those portions, also provide Council with a recommendation on the ROW vacation. After two meetings, former Commissioner Kenworthy convinced the Commission they couldn’t make a decision on anything until the matter of the ROW was decided. So the MPD, already in clear violation of the LMC governing action, was put on hold again and Deer Valley came before Council with its ROW petition early this year. Council was crystal clear for a while; Deer Valley’s application didn’t come close to satisfying good cause or net tangible community benefit, two conditions of a row vacation as provided for in Park City Resolution 8-98. But then rather than follow standard process and leave it to Deer Valley to make changes or go for a vote, someone in this building decided to invite the applicant behind closed doors and enter into protracted negotiations. This application violated code for inaction. And now because of the City’s own ill-advised process, you want to rush this entire community and your Council to a pressured vote on a deal, the terms for which you cannot fully explain today and say you will not fully explain until after a vote. Resolution 8-98 says “this policy shall not be construed as creating a right or entitlement…but shall be advisory for the Planning Commission and the City Council to utilize when exercising their legislative discretion in evaluating the merits of a vacation petition.” Except that the Planning Commission has been removed from this process… The resolution says, “although the City Council will give significant weight to the Planning Commission recommendation, the ultimate decision to vacate or not rests with the Council” Except that you have no majority opinion from your Commission in writing. Summit County legal precedent affirms resolutions and ordinances carry the same weight as the LMC. comment: Opposition To the Council and Planning Commission: This is in response to the December 14, 2023, Agenda, Item No 1 under Old Business re the Deer Valley Right-of-Way Vacation, 1. The Letter of Intent (LOI) (and the LOI Resolution ) is MEANINGLESS. By definition, an LOI is not binding and creates no obligations whatsoever. Deer Valley is not agreeing to anything. The last paragraph of the proposed LOI, states: "PCMC and DVR acknowledge and agree that this Letter is a statement of the parties' intent to negotiate and complete a PPPA on the basis set forth in this Letter and neither party will be contractually bound to the other, until they have each executed and delivered to the other the mutually acceptable definitive PPPA. This Letter is neither an agreement of the parties nor an offer to enter into an agreement, and this Letter neither creates nor imposes any legal or equitable obligations on either party before the execution of the PPPA."(Bold emphasis added) The public needs to know that there is no binding commitment, and yet in listening to the comments made at the December 5 meeting, several Council members and some members of the public are basing their decision to support on this DVR “promise”. Yet, the LOI and the draft Resolution and proposed Ordinance do not contain a binding commitment. 2. Comments following the City's argument on Dec. 5, 2023, that a right of way cannot be sold and has no value. DVR is offering $15 million without being asked, so we know the ROW has significant value. It's misleading to argue the ROW has no value because the land on which the ROW sits cannot be sold. That's comparing apples to oranges. Every lawyer who completed real property law in the first year of law school knows that a "property interest" has value. Easements and rights of way are all tangible property interests and have value. The City's lawyer and manager are not being objective here. 3. The claim that "good cause" is a legislative decision is legal mumbo jumbo and designed to undermine and suppress public criticism that is contrary to the Council’s views. While an appellate court when reviewing a “legislative decision” will give deference to a city council's determination, that doesn't mean the Council can do whatever it wants or unilaterally define what is good cause. “Broad discretion” cannot ignore or supplant the Council’s duty under the Utah Code. Yet, that was the argument put forth by the City attorney on December 5 – to state it is council that will decide what is good cause even if you have a legitimate opposing view. The City's obligation is clear under the UTAH CODE that states there is a two-fold requirement (1) finding of good cause AND (2) neither a PUBLIC INTEREST nor "any person" will be materially injured by the vacation. If a single person is materially injured, then the requirement is not met. 4. The Draft Ordinance ignores the many public comments about the impact on the public interest and it does not give any deference to the individual complaints of the loss of the use of the right of way or the complaints from increased and changing traffic patterns. There have been public comments about the unknown extent of the taking of land to support the development that directly results from the ROW vacation. Any loss of use or land is a material injury to a person’s property interest. Yet the Ordinance states just the opposite and claims no one has made a claim of injury. You have not listened to the public comments. 5. The Draft Ordinance does not support certain Recitals and the “Good Cause” statement is MISLEADING because it is not supported. The Ordinance states as point no. 1 of Good Cause “Petitioners provided valuable consideration in the form of $15,000,000 dollars to Park City, for the purposes detailed herein.” This is misleading because: A. DVR has not provided ANY consideration and it also has not made a binding promise to provide any money to Park City. B. It is written in the past or present tense as if the money was paid. This is an expectation. In basic contract law – it is a failure of consideration. It’s an empty promise. If DVR refuses pay or sign a final agreement, the City has no ability to enforce it. C. DVR's obligations for the $15 million is not addressed in the draft LOI, LOI Resolution or Ordinance. We cannot be present and traveling the day of the meeting. We oppose both the current ROW vacation and the non-binding LOI and current draft Ordinance. There is no reason to rush into any decision. McNamara, Owners, In The Trees Zip Code 84060

comment: make these comments a part of the Public Record. December 13, 2023 Dear Mayor Worel and City Councilors, Thank you for your time and consideration. I am writing to specifically comment on items presented at the December 5 City Council meeting and items included as part of the December 14 packet related to the Deer Valley ROW Vacation Petition. City Council Staff Report, Deer Valley Right-of-Way Vacation Petition Regarding a Portion of Deer Valley Drive at Snow Park Village, Date: December 14, 2023 In the City Council Staff Report, “John Robertson, the City Engineer confirms the following: Upon evaluating the exchange of replacement right-of-way, the retention of existing public utility easements and required new utility easements, and the Streets Master Plan, the City Engineer determined the proposed area of the right-of-way vacation to no longer have significant utility to the City.” Per Resolution 8-98, (d) Utility of existing right of way, “The City shall typically dispose of a public right of way only when the right of way is no longer of significant utility to the City.” The proposed area of ROW vacation currently has significant utility to the City. It is 2.6 acres of land that is regularly used by transit, vehicles, bikes and pedestrians. The current transit drop-off and City electric bike sharing location are located in this area, as well as the current pedestrian and bicycle paths which are widely used. City staff has commented that this drop off is closer than the proposed drop off which encourages transit usage. A ROW may be replaced with the dedication of a new ROW. The ROW Vacation Petition from January 2022 seeks to dedicate public ROW along Doe Pass Road. The proposed Ordinance Vacating a Portion of Deer Valley Drive reads, “At the time of recording the Final Plat, Deer Valley shall grant permanent access rights to Park City over Doe Pass Road.” This is not a dedication or exchange of replacement right of way. This needs to be clarified before the City Council can vote on the ROW vacation. Exhibit A: Applicant’s ROW Vacation Petition The ROW Vacation Petition from January 2022 is included as an exhibit. The ROW Vacation Petition was initially filed in September 2021 and revised in January 2022 with updated maps and legal descriptions. Per the September 21 petition, as required by Utah Code, owners directly adjacent or within 300 feet of the vacation area were notified. Exhibit B: Frequently Asked Questions Good Cause - As noted Good Cause is defined by the City’s LMC as “Providing public amenities and benefits, resolving existing issues and non-conformities, addressing issues related to density, promoting excellent and sustainable design, utilizing best planning and design practices, preserving the character of the neighborhood and of Park City and furthering the health, safety, and welfare of the Park City community.” The current MPD application and ROW vacation petition do not meet these criteria. Development Density – Deer Valley is limited to 209.75 unit equivalents per the MPD, but the right of way vacation increases the development footprint. The original site is 14.93 acres. The new proposed site with the ROW vacation is 17.53 acres. That is an increase in the site footprint of over 17%. comment: I am writing to voice my opinion against the vacation of roadway along the Deer Valley Loop as petitioned by Altera Corporation in its present form for the following reasons: Park City Municipal Corporation is receiving very little, if nothing in return for their gifting of land to Alterra. It should be the responsibility of Alterra Corp. to move their customers and their employees to and from their place of business. Also, it is Alterra’s responsibility to house their employees or pay wages that enable those employees to afford to live in the community. It should not fall upon the taxpayers of this city to subsidize Alterra’s operation. Alterra Corporation paying money to the city for transportation and housing shifts the burden of those programs away from Alterra and onto the taxpayers. The city will also have the burden for maintaining and administering those operations at additional taxpayer expense. When the money runs out and the infrastructure ages, only the city will have the responsibility to come up with needed funds. Alterra initially estimated an additional 3500 vehicle trips per day as a result of this project. Those numbers may be true for the first season but then will likely be exceeded - there is no penalty for their underestimating the actual impact. The traffic as a result of Deer Valley operations already exceeds what was expected for their current size. PC Muni states a desire to become a green city in the near future; how can the city say this in good faith if it is promoting additional auto traffic? Alterra Corp. should be required to undo the harm they have already done to this city by permanently cutting vehicle trips by 3500/day. The traffic plan is not acceptable for a residential neighborhood. If the roadway near the resort is given to Alterra for their expansion, then Doe Pass Road should be turned over to the city to realign the Deer Valley Loop. All Deer Valley Resort traffic should be circulated within the confines of Alterra property and cycled back to the western portion of Deer Valley Loop so as to minimize traffic, noise, and air quality impacts to nearby residential areas. All proposed traffic controlling devices (traffic lights) should be on Alterra property so that local residential traffic can continue to flow unimpeded. In return for approval of their expansion plans, Alterra should abandon plans for an additional phase of development at the resort base. The land that will not be developed in this phase (what is now the northern-most parking lot) should be given to the city as likekind compensation for the roadway vacation the be designated as open space or a park for the benefit of local citizenry. I believe the road vacation in favor of DVC is inevitable, but I believe that the citizens of this town need adequate compensation and assurances that the project will at the very least have a neutral impact on our quality of life.

This letter of intent does not satisfy the obligation our city leaders have to our community to secure a reasonable exchange of compensation. Our community requests our leaders secure an actual 15 million dollar payment from Deer Valley to Park City now in order to fulfill a reasonable compensation exchange. Exhibit B from the December 14 agenda packet states Deer Valley currently has 1,700 day skier parking stalls. This is incorrect. Currently Deer Valley has 1,482 day skier parking stalls as stated in the Fehr Peers report and prior agenda packets. A 20% reduction in day skier parking would be 1,185 day skier parking stalls vs the 1,360 day skier stalls Deer Valley is proposing. 1,360 day skier stalls represents an 8.23% reduction vs the 20% reduction negotiated and announced. I request our city leadership hold Deer Valley to their promise of a 20% reduction in day parking which would be 1,185 day skier parking stalls. The PPPA announcement prior to the final City Council vote on the ROW vacation petition has the effect of tipping the scales. Our City Councilors are being asked to vote independently on the ROW vacation while their employer, Park City, has announced a PPPA with Deer Valley. There is now significant pressure on our City Councilors to support the PPPA vs supporting the needs of community members in 84060. At the November 30th meeting our community first learned our elected officials designated to represent our community on the ROW vacation petition spent months partnering with Deer Valley to help unlock what terms Park City may deem potential good cause for the pending ROW vacation petition. The community does not support the ROW vacation petition so why did our elected officials designated to work on this issue choose this path? June 15th was the last time our community heard an update on the status of the ROW vacation petition conversations. We were kept in the dark for 5 months. Our elected officials prior to June 15th made efforts to be inclusive and transparent with our community. I was disappointed to learn the most important period in this application process was kept a secret. For future decisions of this significance, please know transparency is sharing what is happening with an application promptly. The loss of transparency on the ROW vacation petition over the last few months lead to our community feeling blindsided by the PPPA announced on November 30th. In real time at the meeting our leaders designated to work on this issue seemed genuinely surprised our community was not grateful for the deal. Our elected leaders should not allow Deer Valley to expand outside of their entitled development footprint. This critical section of road is of significant utility for pedestrian use, cycling and convenient skier and day care drop-off and pick-up. This road is an integral part of daily life in our neighborhood. We are setting precedent with this ROW vacation petition decision and other developers are waiting to see what happens. Questions: 1. 1. Why wasn’t the ROW vacation petition voted on last year or early this year when it was clear our community supported Deer Valley’s existing development rights but not the ROW vacation petition? 2. 2. If Deer Valley did not offer good cause with their ROW vacation petition from the start, why did our city officials feel obligated to continue to partner with Deer Valley to search for potential good cause? 3. 3. If the ROW vacation petition is denied, are there alternative courses of action on the table being discussed with Deer Valley that could potentially be worse for Park City? If so, please share those details with the community. We deserve to know why it appears we are on the verge of granting Deer Valley a larger contiguous footprint for their development without good cause. Finally, I am reiterating my request for our City Council to vote no on the ROW vacation petition. I support the existing development rights of Deer Valley and nothing more. Sincerely, Allison Kitching

comment: As a Lower Deer Valley condominium owner just across the street from the bottom of the parking lot to be developed, it has been with keen interest I have followed the process of the submission of plans as well as the petition for the ROW vacation. For the record, I am in favor of the base village being developed, however whether it is or is not, Deer Valley will continue to be successful. But if the ROW vacation is approved under the current terms proposed, my fear is that it will cause great material injury in the form of even more frequent daily traffic jams on Deer Valley Dr E - and we won't even know until it is too late. As an outside observer, from my perspective the communication and arguments set forth by PTL have been nonjudgmental, supportive of the development, and have shown concern for the public good as well as the compliance with Utah laws as noted repeatedly. On the other hand, the communication from Alterra has not offered anything new of substance ever since the plan submission of about a year ago. And the communication of the Council has been mostly silent until recently. Neither has adequately addressed the real concerns of the public. This behavior is concerning at best. Further, I am disturbed to read about the "partnership" and the suggestion that the ROW vacation will be approved by council at the upcoming December 14 meeting. Many members of the public have spoken to indicate real material injury will occur. The statutes are also clear that a vacation cannot be approved in such an instance. I have seen nothing communicated to indicate that the vacation will not cause material injury. In the agenda for December 14, it is noted "After reviewing all of the above, including past staff reports and public input, at their City Council meeting, a majority of the Council discussed good cause for the vacation and that the vacation does not cause any material injury..." JUST BECAUSE THE MAJORITY OF THE COUNCIL DISCUSSED THEN STATED THE VACATION DOES NOT CAUSE MATERIAL INJURY DOES NOT MEAN IT IN FACT DOES NOT CAUSE MATERIAL INJURY!!! Common sense tells me the burden of proof is on proving there will be no material injury. Let me go on record to further say that I suspect I will suffer material injury if the ROW vacation occurs, but I will not know for sure until the project is finished. Council members deciding it will not cause injury is not proof. Furthermore, the "Public Private Partnership" appears to be simply a way to justify the Council not following State Law with regards to the ROW vacation and an attempt to persuade members of the public that they negotiated something substantial in return. Setting aside the two items that were "agreed upon" that were already part of the plan up for approval (why are they even in the LOI?), $15 million dollars toward "improving transportation" is a drop in the bucket compared to the money Alterra will spend to develop the mixed use base village. $150 million is a more appropriate amount to consider. Better yet, I suggest Council require that a tunnel be built underneath the proposed ski beach in the same path as the current ROW. That way the ROW vacation will not be necessary and regardless of the cost to Alterra, it will appease the overwhelming public objection to the ROW vacation and render the material injury issue moot. As the author Harvey McCay stated in his book Swim With The Sharks Without Being Eaten Alive , I paraphrase - "If you can buy your way out of a problem, you don't have a problem anymore - you simply have an expense". Council - please do not approve the ROW vacation or the Public Private Partnership at this time. If you acquiesce now, you will not be serving your constituents nor the long term good of Deer Valley homeowners and residents. You can and should get A LOT more from the developer. It's your job.

comment: In 1986 I had the fortune of being introduced to Park City for our annual spring break ski trip. Our family immediately fell in love with all that Park City represented. Early years PCRM was our home mountain. Back then we could pull into the parking garage below the resort, ride the elevator up a couple floors and walk 50-100 steps to the ticket counter and the slopes. Most of the time without a cost for parking. How convenient that was. Fast forward to 1992 when we purchased our next property in Lower Deer Valley, Deer Valley became our home mountain. Wow, the Deer Valley difference. We all know the many things that are part of that DV Difference, as I age and my knees deteriorate, I find one of the greatest differences is being dropped off, walking 30 steps to the carpenter lift and up the mountain I go. Sounds like limiting principles but it’s becoming a fact for my old body. Without the loop, how will this experience change? Listening to the testimony last week, I really believe that there is nothing wrong with the city granting the vacation of the road. The land belongs to DV, safety issues have been reviewed, and if DV wants to mess up the entry experience for their customers, they should be allowed to do so (hopefully they won’t). I will miss those 30 steps to the slopes and so will many others. It is time for that area to be developed. It is time to make improvements to the parking lot. Walking from the end of the lot or waiting for the tram is a good experience but can be improved. Adding walking sidewalks, escalators, and other improvements will improve the parking experience. Lastly, it is time to get ready for 2034. Let’s build this project. The transportation hub looks to be a well thought out improvement. But unanswered questions include, how many steps will it be from Grade 1 to Grad 4. Will it be stairs, escalators, or ramps. Will it be 30 steps or 400 steps to get to that first lift. Will my DV direct shuttle drop me at the transportation center or at the new loop that looks to remain 30 steps. If I’m being dropped off at the transportation hub, how will the DV Difference manifest to get me and my equipment to the slopes. Maybe sharing some of these answers will help those who are fighting for the loop feel better. I look forward to progress and hope these access issues have been well thought out. Each year I venture out to our neighboring slopes. It’s crazy to have to park on the highway in front of Snowbird because parking is full. Same for Brighton. It’s always felt different at DV. I wish DV success, I thank the city council, plan commission and all who have worked hard to vet this project. It is bound to be great for all. Lastly, I too agree with several of last week’s speakers, bring back BYOB to the concert series . Happy skiing and thanks for reading this. comment: This is in response to the , Agenda, Item No 1 under Old Business re the Deer Valley Right-of-Way Vacation 1. The Letter of Intent (LOI) (and the LOI Resolution ) is MEANINGLESS. By definition, an LOI is not binding and creates no obligations whatsoever. Deer Valley is not agreeing to anything. The last paragraph of the proposed LOI, states: "PCMC and DVR acknowledge and agree that this Letter is a statement of the parties' intent to negotiate and complete a PPPA on the basis set forth in this Letter and neither party will be contractually bound to the other, until they have each executed and delivered to the other the mutually acceptable definitive PPPA. This Letter is neither an agreement of the parties nor an offer to enter into an agreement, and this Letter neither creates nor imposes any legal or equitable obligations on either party before the execution of the PPPA." The public needs to know that there is no binding commitment, and yet in listening to the comments made at the December 5 meeting, several Council members and some members of the public are basing their decision to support on this DVR “promise”. Yet, the LOI and the draft Resolution and proposed Ordinance do not contain a binding commitment. 2. Comments following the City's argument on Dec. 5, 2023, that a right of way cannot be sold and has no value. DVR is offering $15 million without being asked, so we know the ROW has significant value. It's misleading to argue the ROW has no value because the land on which the ROW sits cannot be sold. That's comparing apples to oranges. Every lawyer who completed real property law in the first year of law school knows that a "property interest" has value. Easements and rights of way are all tangible property interests and have value. The City's lawyer and manager are not being objective here. 3. The claim that "good cause" is a legislative decision is legal mumbo jumbo and designed to undermine and suppress public criticism that is contrary to the Council’s views. While an appellate court when reviewing a “legislative decision” will give deference to a city council's determination, that doesn't mean the Council can do whatever it wants or unilaterally define what is good cause. “Broad discretion” cannot ignore or supplant the Council’s duty under the Utah Code. Yet, that was the argument put forth by the City attorney on December 5 – to state it is council that will decide what is good cause even if you have a legitimate opposing view. The City's obligation is clear under the Utah Code that states there is a two-fold requirement (1) finding of good cause AND (2) neither a PUBLIC INTEREST nor "any person" will be materially injured by the vacation. If a single person is materially injured, then the requirement is not met. 4. The Draft Ordinance ignores the many public comments about the impact on the public interest and it does not give any deference to the individual complaints of the loss of the use of the right of way or the complaints from increased and changing traffic patterns. There have been public comments about the unknown extent of the taking of land to support the development that directly results from the ROW vacation. Any loss of use or land is a material injury to a person’s property interest. Yet the Ordinance states just the opposite and claims no one has made a claim of injury. You have not listened to the public comments. 5. The Draft Ordinance does not support certain Recitals and the “Good Cause” statement is MISLEADING because it is not supported. The Ordinance states as point no. 1 of Good Cause: “Petitioners provided valuable consideration in the form of $15,000,000 dollars to Park City, for the purposes detailed herein.” This is misleading because: A. DVR has not provided ANY consideration and it also has not made a binding promise to provide any money to Park City. B. It is written in the past or present tense as if the money was paid. This is an expectation. In basic contract law – it is a failure of consideration. It’s an empty promise. If DVR refuses pay or sign a final agreement, the City has no ability to enforce it. C. DVR's obligations for the $15 million is not addressed in the draft LOI, LOI Resolution or Ordinance. We cannot be present and traveling the day of the meeting. We are not opposed to development on the original site. However, we oppose both the current ROW vacation and the non-binding LOI and current draft Ordinance. There is no reason to rush into any decision until we see a binding promise and we should consider alternate proposals.
source: eComment (written; published verbatim in council meeting minutes)

comment: I have lived in Park City from 2001-2008 and then again from 2015 to present. My husband, daughter and I are full time residents in Park Meadows in Park City. I am a physical therapist and have commuted to Salt Lake City for many years for my job. Over the years I have witnessed the road kill along SR224 and I-80. In 2003 I had a patient who was involved in a life altering accident from hitting a moose on I-80 on his way to Salt Lake City from Park City. He went from being a college football player to learning to be independent as a quadriplegic. I appreciate all that the Save People Save Wildlife organization has done to try to prevent more accidents on our roads. Once the fences went up along I-80 there was a huge decrease in the amount of dead animals along the road. I agree that the fencing needs to be continued along SR224 into town. But there also has to be a way for these animals to migrate across SR224. I believe a wildlife overpass or underpass would be the best solution. We cannot turn a blind eye to what is going on. As we grow we have to consider our environment and the animals that we share it with. We saved Bonanza Flats. We paid to prevent Treasure from building. Surely considering all that was spent on those 2 projects alone I would think we could come up with a viable solution to this issue that is extremely important to our town and our county. Please make this a priority. I will leave you with an article from the Texas Monthly about how Texas has seen human and animal lives saved with such bridges. https://www.texasmonthly.com/travel/texaswildlife-crossings-saving-lives-and-money/#

comment: Wildlife are part of our community and we need to help them survive in Park City and Summit County by providing safe passage over/under SR 224. We have developed, and we live in, their environment; SR 224 bisects, and presents a deadly gauntlet across, the feeding, calving, and migration paths of Deer, Moose, and Elk. Wildlife enrich our lives, our community, and enhances tourism and the tourist experience in Park City. City Council members are no doubt aware that a few mile stretch of SR 224 has the 5th highest incidence of vehicle/animal collisions in the state of Utah. This grim statistic will get worse with the widening of SR 224 (up to 35% wider in places), as proposed by High Valley Transit, as there is no plans for the safe passage of animals in the proposal. It is up to us, the citizens and City Council of Park City, to create an overpass/underpass for the safe passage of wildlife, either as a requirement for the HVT proposal and/or through public/private funding. It is difficult for any city to balance growth and development while maintaining its character. In the case of Park City, this is especially true, as we want to project a rural feel and preserve and project our history. Wildlife are part of our history and create a rural feel; they warrant our concern and protection. An improvement to the existing underpass to the McPolin Barn would be an unnoticeable and lowest cost means to provide a safe passage for the animals. Further, an overcrossing would be the best solution to encourage safe passage for wildlife. Placed at the northern end of Quarry Mountain, an overcrossing would serve as a gateway or entrance to inner Park City, exposing the rural view, deemphasizing the “urban highway” proposed by HVT, and would partly obscure the 80’ high voltage towers and lines recently installed on the East side of SR 224. While these are two solutions, there are other possibilities along SR 224 to save wildlife. Many Park City residents and taxpayers share the views expressed here; please consider the wildlife in our community. I ask the City Council to make a recommendation on this topic and support the creation of a safe passage for wildlife across SR 224.

comment: You can google and you will instantly find that PB is – again – the fastest growing sport in America. PB is especially popular in Utah, with many articles reporting that Utah has more PB players than any other state. I urge you to ask your Rec Department the following questions: 1. How many hours are dedicated to tennis in the main building (4 courts) and how many to PB? 2. How many weekday “prime time” hours (9 AM to 6 PM) are dedicated to tennis in the bubble and how many to PB? 3. What are the dedicated hours when PB players can book a bubble court? 4. Does the allocation of hours for court reservations for tennis compared to the allocation of hours when PB players can reserve a court accurately reflect the number of MARC patrons who participate in each sport? 5. How many MARC patrons play tennis compared to the number who play PB? 6. Why hasn’t the MARC asked its customers if they like the current allocation of court reservation times? Each of the last 3 years, the Rec Department has reported to the City Council to “justify” the arbitrary, unfair, and unjustified preference given to tennis players. In 2021, they said the disparity was based on revenue: tennis produced far more revenue than PB, and thus it got far more hours. This is untrue. Tennis produces more revenue because tennis gets more hours. So in 2022, the justification changed. Tennis gets more hours because the MARC is a “purpose built” facility, and the purpose for which it was built was tennis. This is true, but the MARC was built as a private tennis club (the Racket Club). It failed, the facility was purchased by Park City Municipal Corporation, and rebranded as the Municipal Athletic and Recreation Center (MARC). Surely the use of a public facility cannot and should not be dictated by its purpose when it was a private club! And so in 2023, the rationale changed again. The Rec Dept said it met with the Park City Pickleball Club, and the Club “endorsed” the winter hours play schedule, and “agreed” that PB and tennis should not be played side by side in the bubble. Again, this was untrue. The PCPB Club never endorsed those hours, and the Club has continually sought both more access and equal opportunity to book bubble courts, first come, first served, with tennis and PB played side by side. This brings us to March, 2024. Once again the Rec Department has given 100% of the use of the 4 courts in the main building to tennis, and the overwhelming majority of bubble hours (and all the “prime time” weekday hours) to tennis as well. PB players get only the most undesirable times (typically 6-8 AM and after 6 PM some weeknights). The job of government is to equitably allocate scarce resources among competing stakeholders. In this case, you have failed miserably. The MARC continues to operate as if it were a private tennis club, catering to the wishes of tennis players, and ignoring the explosive growth in PB. Sure, they throw PB players a few crumbs: leftover courts that tennis players don’t book are then “released” to PB (and typically they are snapped up quickly). But prime time weekday access is nil. I urge you to take immediate action to remedy this injustice. Here are some concrete steps you can take: 1. Allocate the 4 courts in the main building to tennis, and the 3 bubble courts to PB, or 2. Alternate days (one day tennis gets the main building, PB gets the bubble, then switch), or 3. Make the bubble a “first come, first served

comment: My family and I are full-time residents of the Iron Canyon neighborhood; we have a kindergartener and second grader who attend Parley's Park Elementary. I'm reaching out to express my objection to the annexation petition to create three single-family lots within our Iron Canyon and Thaynes Canyon neighborhoods. I share the concerns articulated in several letters from my fellow Iron Canyon residents. The addition of multiple new driveways exiting onto Iron Canyon Drive poses safety risks. As a parent of young children, I am concerned about exacerbating the hazards along this road, which already presents challenges in terms of its shape, grade, and width. I regularly observe vehicles encountering difficulties, such as getting stuck or sliding off the road, and I know from personal experience that this location's sight lines are already a challenge without additional vehicles entering and exiting along it. Furthermore, Iron Canyon has only two access points to the rest of Park City. Introducing more driveways would heighten safety concerns for daily use and emergencies. A single driveway placed in a safer location, such as on Payday Drive, and serving a single-family home, would be more prudent for the neighborhood and the city. The proposed lot sizes outlined in the petition would deviate significantly from the established norms of Iron Canyon and Thaynes Canyon. Such a departure would disrupt the character and aesthetic of our communities, which were meticulously planned with principles that this proposed development would undermine. A single home on a lot size consistent with those of existing properties in our neighborhoods would be more appropriate. The assertion that the common area should be included as developable land is misleading. While adjustments to land use may be warranted as circumstances evolve, proposals for outright contractions require exceptional justification, which this proposal lacks. I am aware that you have received letters from some of my fellow residents. The volume in correspondence from Iron Canyon and neighboring Thaynes residents may be low due to varying levels of engagement with local affairs. But if this annexation petition were more well known, opposition would likely be unanimous. Approving the annexation petition would establish an unfavorable precedent that fails to address broader community needs or represent the interests of city residents effectively. I ask that the city reject the annexation petition and end its review process. The applicant should reconsider excluding the Iron Canyon common area from the proposal and explore alternative options for developing a single-family home without access to and from Iron Canyon Drive. Thank you for your attention to this matter, and for your dedication to serving Park City.

comment: A neighbor brought this development proposal to my attention. I did not receive notice even thought my property abuts two parcels of land labelled as IC-Misc. comment: I am writing in opposition to the annexation petition to create three single-family lots in our Iron Canyon and Thaynes Canyon neighborhoods. I concur with the detailed concerns outlined in many of my Iron Canyon neighbors' letters. First, the sizes of the proposed lots would significantly deviate from those of Iron Canyon and Thaynes Canyon. Such a divergent variance would conflict with the character and landscape of these communities, each of which was designed with principles that would be undermined by this incompatible proposed development. One home on a lot size consistent with those of other lots in these neighborhoods would be appropriate. Second, adding multiple new driveways exiting onto Iron Canyon Drive would undermine safety. As the father of young children, I do not want additional risk compounding along this section of road, which already creates problems in its shape, width, grade, drainage, and visibility. I regularly witness vehicles getting stuck, sliding off the road, or struggling with its sight lines. Moreover, the entire Iron Canyon neighborhood has only two points of ingress and egress to the rest of Park City. Increasing driveway density would introduce additional hazards in general for daily use and especially at times of need. A single driveway that would be placed in a safer location (such as on Payday Drive), and as important, that would generate traffic consistent with that of a single family home (versus three), would be in the best interest of the neighborhood and the City. Third, the self-serving interpretation that the common area was intended and should be included as developable land is misleading. Pursuing shifts in land use may be appropriate as needs and markets evolve, but proposals with outright contractions require unique circumstances -- and this proposal does not come close to meeting that standard. Finally, while you may receive letters from only a subset of Iron Canyon and nearby Thaynes residents given varying levels of engagement in local matters, if every Iron Canyon resident were polled about this proposed development and actually responded, opposition would be nearly universal for reasons such as those above. Approval of the annexation petition would set an ugly precedent that would fail to serve broader community needs as well as the community members the City represents. I request that this annexation petition be denied and the review process be terminated. The applicant should exclude our Iron Canyon common area and examine annexing the tract for development of a single family home that does not have access to and from Iron Canyon Drive. Thank you for your consideration, and we appreciate all you do for Park City.

comment: I have been a home owner on Iron Canyon Drive for the last 20 years and I am opposed to the above petition. The petition combines a Summit County parcel (outlined in blue on Exhibit B) with the adjacent Park City parcels, and then subdivides the resulting property into three lots. Iron Canyon Drive is the entry road into our Iron Canyon subdivision and is also used by many of the residents of Aspen Springs. The strip of land that runs along the road (a portion of Parcel IC-MISC) was platted in 1983 as part of the Iron Canyon subdivision and was represented as being common area (see Exhibit A for the actual separate boundaries of this entire parcel). This is confirmed by the legal description associated with each lot of Iron Canyon according to the Summit County Assessor which includes the notation “COMMON AREA IS NOW BEING ASSESSED UNDER IC-MISC.” The parcels contain a monument sign identifying the area as Iron Canyon, consistent with its intended use as common area. Title to Parcel IC-MISC was held by the Boyer Company as the developer of the Iron Canyon subdivision and had been so held for almost 40 years on behalf of the Iron Canyon lot owners (a Homeowners Association was never created to take title). In December, 2022, the property was conveyed by the Boyer Company to an entity called the Boyer Robbins JV with a description in the deed which states “NOTE: THIS PROPERTY WAS DETERMINED NOT TO BE COMMON AREA.” This statement and the transfer of the property are not consistent with the long held understanding of the use of the property. Who determined this was not Iron Canyon common area? It was not those of us who live in Iron Canyon. It was not Park City. It was not Summit County. For 40 years this has been common area. Whether there can be found some legal basis for the transfer or not, it is the long held understanding and representation that the property was common area and therefore not subject to further development. I do not oppose allowing the landowner of SS-104-B constructing a single dwelling on the property. Nor do I oppose the annexation of SS-104-B into Park City. Construction of one dwelling on SS-104-B is entirely consistent with the neighborhood. Iron Canyon Drive serves as the entry and exit road for our Iron Canyon subdivision. It has a posted speed limit of 15 mph between Payday Drive and Delta Drive. This is because of the “S” curves and the grade of the road. The road is steeper and narrower than most other residential roads, has no curbs and gutters or sidewalks. In spite of the posted speed limit, there has been at least one out of control vehicle slide off on this section of the road every year for each of the last 30 years. These accidents usually occur by vehicles sliding off to the south as they go around the middle curve, but there have also been slide offs onto the subject property. Tow trucks are often required to extract the vehicles due to the terrain on either side of the road. Vehicles traveling around the northern most curve of the road cannot see oncoming traffic until they have entered the curve. In short this stretch of narrow road is hazardous. Furthermore, our children walk up the road after being dropped off by the school bus which stops on Payday Drive. If three parcels were to be developed as proposed, with driveway access to those parcels from Iron Canyon Drive this road would become even more hazardous. I do not want to see driveway access to Iron Canyon Drive even if a single house was constructed on SS-104-B. The staff report proposes two alternatives for the City Council to consider. I would like to see the City Council select the alternative to deny this annexation petition, terminating the review process. Thank you for the opportunity to provide input on this important matter to all Thaynes Canyon residents.

In December, 2022, the property was conveyed by the Boyer Company to an entity called the Boyer Robbins JV with a description in the deed which states “NOTE: THIS PROPERTY WAS DETERMINED NOT TO BE COMMON AREA.” This statement and the transfer of the property are not consistent with the long held understanding of the use of the property. Who determined this was not Iron Canyon common area? It was not those of us who live in Iron Canyon. It was not Park City. It was not Summit County. For 40 years this has been common area. Whether there can be found some legal basis for the transfer or not, it is the long held understanding and representation that the property was common area and therefore not subject to further development. It is just not right to take Iron Canyon common area and place it into the JV. I do not oppose allowing the landowner of SS-104-B constructing a single dwelling on the property. Nor do I oppose the annexation of SS-104-B into Park City. Construction of one dwelling on SS-104-B is entirely consistent with the neighborhood. Iron Canyon Drive serves as the entry and exit road for our Iron Canyon subdivision. It has a posted speed limit of 15 mph between Payday Drive and Delta Drive. This is because of the “S” curves and the grade of the road. The road is steeper and narrower than most other residential roads, has no curbs and gutters or sidewalks. In spite of the posted speed limit, there has been at least one out of control vehicle slide off on this section of the road every year for each of the last 30 years. These accidents usually occur by vehicles sliding off to the south as they go around the middle curve, but there have also been slide offs onto the subject property. Tow trucks are often required to extract the vehicles due to the terrain on either side of the road. Vehicles traveling around the northern most curve of the road cannot see oncoming traffic until they have entered the curve. In short this stretch of narrow road is hazardous. Furthermore, our children walk up the road after being dropped off by the school bus which stops on Payday Drive. If three parcels were to be developed as proposed, with driveway access to those parcels from Iron Canyon Drive this road would become even more hazardous. I do not want to see driveway access to Iron Canyon Drive even if a single house was constructed on SS-104-B. The staff report proposes two alternatives for the City Council to consider. I would like to see the City Council select the alternative to deny this annexation petition, terminating the review process. The City Council may want to instruct the applicant to bring back a petition that excludes our Iron Canyon common area, annexes tract SS-104-B into Park City, includes a single family home and does not have access from Iron Canyon Drive. Thank you for the opportunity to provide input on this important matter to Iron Canyon residents.
source: eComment (written; published verbatim in council meeting minutes)

comment: I am writing to you to let you know I support the comments submitted below by Richard Pick. I am not opposed to the annexation of the parcel and building one home on the lot. However, the entrance to the property should not be from Iron Canyon Drive. Iron Canyon Drive and Iron Mountain Drive are very narrow roads, and become even more narrow in winter with the snowfall and snow removal. The road is a tertiary road for snowplowing, and can be quite slippery in winter. There are no gutters, no sidewalks, no shoulders to speak of except for some gravel, and the “S” curves are blind corners and therefore can be dangerous. I had a “grab your heart experience” some time ago when traveling downhill, going around the northern most “S

comment: We are writing in opposition to the subject petition, and in support of the e-mail sent to you on by our neighbor Richard Pick. As detailed in Mr. Pick’s e-mail to you, the petition combines a Summit County parcel with the adjacent Park City parcels, and then subdivides the resulting property into three lots. Iron Canyon Drive is the entry road into the Iron Canyon subdivision, where we purchased a home in trust for our family (including generations to come) more than five years ago. The strip of land that runs along the road (a portion of Parcel IC-MISC) was platted in 1983 as part of the Iron Canyon subdivision and was represented as being common area. The parcels contains a monument sign identifying the area as Iron Canyon, consistent with its intended use as common area. For 40 years this has been common area. As such, it is the long held understanding and representation that the property was common area and therefore not subject to further development. It is just not right to take Iron Canyon common area and place it into a privately held joint venture for development for private use (and/or for development and sale with the profits being reaped by the participants in the new joint venture entity). We do not oppose allowing the landowner of SS-104-B constructing a single dwelling on the property. Nor do we oppose the annexation of SS-104-B into Park City. Construction of one dwelling on SS-104-B is entirely consistent with the neighborhood. Iron Canyon Drive serves as the entry and exit road for our Iron Canyon subdivision. The road is steeper and narrower than most other residential roads, has no curbs and gutters or sidewalks. In short this stretch of narrow road is hazardous. If three parcels were to be developed as proposed, with driveway access to those parcels from Iron Canyon Drive this road would become even more hazardous. I do not want to see driveway access to Iron Canyon Drive even if a single house was constructed on SS-104-B. The road is used by the families that live in the Iron Canyon subdivision as a “walking street”, including to access school transportation and the Rotary park. The staff report proposes two alternatives for the City Council to consider. We would like to see the City Council select the alternative to deny this annexation petition, terminating the review process. The City Council may want to instruct the applicant to bring back a petition that excludes our Iron Canyon common area, annexes tract SS-104-B into Park City, includes a single family home and does not have access from Iron Canyon Drive. Thank you for the opportunity to provide input on this important matter. As noted previously, I fully support the e-mail sent to you by Mr. Pick.

comment: I am writing in opposition to the Annexation Petition to create three SFH lots in Iron Canyon. I have lived in Iron Canyon for 16 years and I agree with Dick Pick's email. I would like to add that the sizes of the proposed new lots are not in keeping with the Iron Canyon neighborhood. I strongly disagree that the Common Area should be included as developable land. It feels like a very underhanded move by Boyer and the JV. However even if the city were to agree with the developer then the proposed three lots would measure a total of 1.73 acres. Each lot would be little more than half an acre and the average lot in the Iron Canyon subdivision is 1.1 acre. Of the 99 lots in the Thaynes neighborhood the average lot is 1.2 acres. Approving this variance would negatively change the landscape of our great neighborhood. Furthermore the proposed driveways are on a very dangerous curve on Iron Canyon Drive. As a 23 year Captain with PCFD, I have personally responded to several accidents on this S-curve. This road isn’t even wide enough to stripe with a center line so the idea of adding three driveways is absurd. I don’t know what the developer is possibly thinking trying to exit three driveways on this dangerous corner. I feel that one home with a driveway that exits closer to the lower section of the Iron Mountain Drive is appropriate. Thank you for considering my views.

comment: I am writing in response to your letter of , providing notice that my home at 2409 Iron Mountain Drive may be affected by a proposed annexation (Robbins Annexation Petition). I oppose this proposed annexation. In addition to the points outlined in Richard Pick's note below, my opposition is also based on the following: Parcel SS-104-B is landlocked. Development of this parcel would require access to Iron Canyon Dr. or another nearby public street, which I believe in any eventuality would require involvement and approval by Park City. As it stands today this parcel cannot be developed and In essence represents open space. This open space is in direct line of sight and part of the view from my home. The proposed annexation would seem to value development (at a greater density than the surrounding neighborhood) at the expense of open space. Arguments that annexation would bring development within Park City regulations seem moot if the parcel cannot be developed without this annexation. Parcel IC-MISC is common space within the Iron Canyon Subdivision. The purpose and past use of this parcel are very important considerations in evaluating this annexation proposal. This parcel obviously was not intended for development but was meant as common space for the benefit of residents, and I would suggest to provide a buffer against further development along Iron Canyon Dr. The proposed annexation would represent a conversion of Iron Canyon Subdivision's common area into a commercial real estate development that would eliminate existing open space and increase the development density of the neighborhood. I would urge the City Council to reject this annexation petition.

comment: I spoke at a Council Meeting several years ago, and over time, my feelings and position have not changed. 1) I am all for E-bikes on the paved path trails. I would suggest something akin to drivers ed at school or at home or some combination thereof to help in creating safe travel (get the kids to slow down) on those paths. 2) I like the joint use of non E-bike and E-bikes on the Clark Ranch and Skyridge trails. You know what to expect if you go there to ride. 3) I am still against E-bikes in Round Valley, DV & PC Mountain Resort trails for several reasons a) E-bike 'Power does not a good and safe rider make'. Years of riding human powered bikes gives one an understanding that 'Technique, Etiquette, Properly Timed and Well Applied Power learned from experience on the trails will not be present if just anyone with an E-bike is allowed to use the trail systems. National Ability Riders should be allowed on the trails with E-bikes (as they are now in PC. They typically have full able bodied associates riding with them in case of emergency, so they are typically supervised) and riders over 65 with E-bikes should be allowed (as they are now on the PC trails, because they are usually more experienced in how to more safely and properly ride and typically understand and comply with better than average etiquette. 4) I would like to see Basin Rec have the same rules as the 84060 for purposes of consistency and equity, but there are of course entitled to making their rules in their jurisdiction. 5) I think more 'Mixed Use' allowing E-bikes on newly built to better handle speeds and the weight and probable decrease in cornering skill levels along with specific trail direction would be best, like the Clark Ranch and Skyridge trails. Build more of them. 6) Lastly, might be hard to do, but have a 'Trail Patrol' to combat illegal E-bike use. You would only be able to use a 'Bully Pulpit' for individual owners of E-bikes and at least chase them off the trails for that day, but if it is an bike shop rental, that logo will be on the bike, the bike shop should be notified that day that one of their renters is in violation of PC Trail Codes and the bike shop should retain their deposit. That deposit would then be split between Mountain Trails to help maintain (fix) trails and the other half goes to support 'Trail Patrol'.
source: eComment (written; published verbatim in council meeting minutes)

comment: As an owner at The Retreat, 1450 Park Ave, I have reviewed the initial proposals for long term assistance for repairs and maintenance and wanted to add some notes to this item. We have actually been in board discussions for the longer terms expenses that we may incur and this potentially could have a negative impact for our community. I am the president on the Board at the Retreat and have been on past HOA boards as well. Some points for this topic: Our development includes only 8 free standing units with solar on 6 units. We are probably amongst the smallest HOA and this has challenges for our monthly expenses for homeowners. With only 8 units, we do not have the advantage other HOA’s have to spread costs over a larger portion of units, so keeping a budget in line and conservative is vitally important to us. Options 4 and 5 are completely unreliable and should not be a consideration for proposed future options. To have the city further involved in a savings fund or merging HOA’s we feel are a terrible idea. For options 1-3. Here are the key challenges for the homeowners. Right now we are restricted on our allowable appreciation for our home, but at the same time there are no caps for future expenses on our units. This causes a potential for a huge gap for a homeowner to step up and sell their unit in the future and be able to retain the appreciation for the home. Also as we discuss the upkeep for the exterior, we are restricted for any upgrades or improvements to the inside of your units. If the kitchen is replaced, we are not allowed to recover that from a future sale. So there is a negative incentive to spend a single dollar for the interior of the units. Other projects do allow improvements to be calculated into a future sale price. Loan funds that will require homeowners to qualify based on current income for all may be an issue for qualifying. For 8 units that cost with a subsidy on interest still will account for 20% of our current budget. Our association is well-managed, we do budget reviews, cost reviews, as should all associations be pro-active in their HOA, that is the key. But with potential expenses that can dilute any equity that is built over time and used for a step up to other housing. Here are some suggestions that we feel should be considered. 1. Allow any needed assessments for the HOA for improvements/repairs to be added to future sale of the property from date of purchase 2. Modify CC&R’s to allow interior improvements of units to be included and be added to future sale of the property from date of purchase. 3. Replace a low interest loan proposal with a grant at 50% of the repair/improvement and the HOA will be responsible for the other 50%. - This removes a 20 year loan on the books with the city - The HOA can then adjust the reserve requirements or with an assessment for the difference - The grant should keep our future sale within the maximum resale price MRP.
source: eComment (written; published verbatim in council meeting minutes)

comment: I ask that you consider this proposal very carefully before we slide further down a slippery slope. Before a person decides to buy a home 'affordable' or not - they have to be forward thinking and consider ALL the expenses this involves, including HOA fees and property taxes. It is his/her responsibility to do so. In Park City, those of us in HOA-managed properties are mostly, if not all, facing increased/increasing dues and special assessments. Park City is building/planning on building hundreds more 'affordable' units. What happens when the buyers of these can no longer afford their HOA dues? Are we going to keep on making funds available from 'somewhere' to bail them out? Requiring additional funds, unfortunately, is not a one time occurrence. Well-managed HOAs should have the reserves to cope with all but major projects. If an HOA has a shortage in reserve funds, it either has to assess members or look to banks for a loan. Lending money is not a risk the City should be taking. In addition, property taxes have greatly increased and will likely continue to do so. What happens when those in 'affordable' properties can't afford to pay them? The City is not a bank and should not be in the loan business.
source: eComment (written; published verbatim in council meeting minutes)

comment: We support current Park City code, limiting e-MTB use on Round Valley single track. In addition, we do not support an e-MTB pilot program, as discussed previously in the mid-August 2109 . More broadly, we support current Park City code throughout City boundaries, with the possible exception of specific resort areas such as Deer Valley's flow trails. Their trails are fairly well differentiated, via design and signage, from trails used by hikers, trail runners, and traditional xc mountain bikers. We appreciate efforts to build e-MTBfriendly trails at Clark Ranch, Sky Ridge, and nearby efforts by Wasatch Trails Foundation in Wasatch County. One request, after talking with several e-bike riders from SLC, would be to strive for consistent e-bike and e-MTB code for PCMC and Basin Rec. The recent interactive trail/route map helps, but may not be known to trail users in SLC/etc. Regarding paved trails, we support speed limits and other safety measures for e-bike use on our paved trail network. If there were a way to separate users on existing parallel pathways (such as along 224) that could be helpful. We're glad to hear about efforts to encourage helmet use, including bike-share participants.
source: eComment (written; published verbatim in council meeting minutes)

comment: I've been looking at the survey results and thinking a bunch over the last few days. I've got plenty of thoughts but I'd like to call the council’s attention to the following. Most people haven't ridden an Ebike on singletrack trails. Only 16% in PC & 20% in the Basin. So many of the survey results are then based on not experiencing the product we're talking about. And that's clear as you hear public comment about more trail damage or bikes zooming uphill at 20 mph. These are not realistic use cases on these bikes. You can read the Single Track Regulations slide in several ways. First is how it seems PCMC staff have overwhelming support for the as is on trails. But there's an alternative view: While the strongest single answer is Support no Ebikes on the basin, 51% are neutral to oppose an all-out ban. You have a huge majority supporting Ebikes on trails with either some or no conditions. And again, is with 80% of respondents never having ridden an emtb on single track trails. ? These answers are based in a lack of knowledge. If anything has been learned through our lived experience of the last 4 years, it should be to listen to experts and not those who lack knowledge. To me what this survey says, most people still don't understand emtbs. But the temperature is changing, emtbs are becoming more accepted. You can see this in the data & on the trials. Our trail system is too vast, with too many entry & exit points to enforce any rule on who can or can't ride them. And is this really how we want to spend resources? Ultimately what you see is user conflict, we should focus time, effort & resources on separating downhill bike traffic from other users. This is the single best tool to tone down user conflict. Seldom Seen & Change Reaction are excellent examples of this in practice. More hiking only trails are another fantastic idea that help users that just don't want to deal with bikes of any kind. I urge the council to focus on the actual problem & not on if/who/how Emtbs are allowed on trail. They are already here, the genie is already out of the bottle and there's no going back. The current "Mobility Disability" is undefined and is a catchall for anyone to get an Emtb on the trails. In the end, if you look at the trends in the industry & on the trial, this is not a question of IF but a question of WHEN. PC is already behind the curve, the longer we debate who/where an EMTB can be ridden, the clouder the definition of an EMTB gets, the more unneeded conflict happens on the trial, the more Deer Valley rents EMTBs at SnowPark base while other shops get a black eye over renting EMTBs.
source: eComment (written; published verbatim in council meeting minutes)

comment: Bonanza Flat Management Plan- Paid Parking Dear Mayor Worel and City Council, I am writing today regarding the Bonanza Flat Open Space paid parking pilot idea being proposed. 93% of the visitors are not Parkites. I’m 100% in support of charging these visitors $10 to park. This user group is not already paying off the Bonanza Flat Open Space Bond with their property taxes. For the 7% of visitors who are Park City residents, I do support the free residential rate via registration of a license plate number or parking code. Additionally, I do support limiting this benefit to only residents paying property taxes contributing to paying off the bond. When I voted for the bond, I did not consider being charged additional fees above what I’m already paying in property taxes. Additional per use parking fees would be charging me twice. Since I use these trails with my dog, I cannot use the shuttle. I do support additional shuttles to the area though because this will decrease the amount of cars parking at these trailheads. I appreciate the ability to park and enjoy this area with my dog.

comment: With regards to the upcoming meeting to discuss plans for Bonanza Flat, I would like to add the following comments. As a resident of neighboring Brighton Estates (and a Summit County property owner), I am subject to all of the traffic, trespassing, and disrespectful activities that take place on Bonanza Flat. I regularly have to direct recreationists off our private property despite signage in our neighborhood that directs them otherwise. 1. I approve of paid parking for the BF lots for the high season. Please do not add any additional parking. 2. Stop further trail development. This is conservation property, not a mountain bike park. There are more than enough trails as it is. 3. The only appropriate trail crossing is near the Y intersection at this location (https://maps.app.goo.gl/hNgF4c8VCEhBnS9d8). I do not see in the staff report where exactly the proposed Pine Canyon crossing location is located, but any further south on Pine Canyon is through a densely foliaged zone of the road where drivers speed with abandon and it also places a crossing and trails too close for comfort to private property. 4. As such, I will ask again, please keep any public trails far from private property to minimize trespassing. We already have so much encroachment and trespass as it is. 5. Please start creating better signage that clearly communicates trails and boundaries. Please help educate the public on safe, appropriate, and respectful use of public lands. To date, I am very disappointed by the signage that has been put up.

comment: As a resident of 84060, and as someone who hikes in the Bonanza Flat area and has seen the congested parking lots, folks parking (and getting tickets) on the road, and witnessed the overuse of the Bloods Lake trail in a few short years, I fully approve of paid parking at the Bonanza Flat parking lots. Critical points however...adding additional parking locations is NOT the answer, it is compounding the problem of recreational overuse of the area. More importantly though, taxpayers in 84060 are already paying for Bonanza Flat, as well as Treasure, in our tax bills every year and need to be exempt from paid parking. Reading the Staff Report, it mentions exempting 84060 would impact the City financially to make it happen, but I don't think so. We already have the Old Town Parking Permit system in place, which cold be expanded to track all license plates residing in 84060 into the same process as is already set up. Parking enforcement has a way to electronically verify a vehicle is allowed to be parked in front of our houses, just add in the ability to do the same at Bonanza Flat. Or, if something visual is needed, we could go back to the sticker or hang tag system that has already been used. Don't recreate the wheel, just play with the spokes of the wheel we already have! Another statement in the Staff report was about expanding Transit to Trails. Another process that I approve of as well, please do expand Transit to Trails to include Empire Pass, the Junction down to Midway, Bloods Lake TH, and Guardsman Pass as planned stops. I actually use all of those locations to begin or end my hikes. But the staff report says it would increase the financial burden on the City...it doesn't have to...beef up the service and CHARGE a nominal fee per passenger per trip. $5 per person to be delivered up is a good amount...and free to ride back down. I have utilized Transit to Trails in the winter, and this is a special service that certainly deserves to have a fee associated with it! As it is, I pay $5 per ride anyways, as I always give the driver a tip...charge us $5 to make the reservation! That also might solve the problems that Transit to Trails has with 'no-shows' -- so many folks make reservations, it's easy, and it's free. And then they decide to blow it off and do something else that day, and the van that was fully reserved often travels up the hill with only 3 or 4 people, not 10. If you make people pay $5 each to reserve a seat in a van, they are more likely to show up. And by charging for the Transit to Trails rides with enhanced service options, it would not be a financial burden on the City. And yes, I would happily pay for it.
source: eComment (written; published verbatim in council meeting minutes)

comment: General Martin Dempsey, retired spoke to Rotary in April. One of his messages was never give up. There is still time to ensure a tunnel is completed under Kearns from the Snow Creek path to the Doubletree. At a minimum I ask that you include in the budget the General Fund amount in the staff report that represents the General Fund contribution. This will provide seed money once the seriousness of the other stakeholders is verified. That eliminates a delay if you have to wait until next year’s budget. That delay will no doubt further increase the cost of the project contributing to the likelihood that it will never be built as well as possibly loosing the other stakeholders. One of those could be the developer of the Doubletree who is before the planning commission, possibly a give/get opportunity. Connectivity at that location provides a bus stop connection to the path to take visitors to “Dans” and more importantly to the liquor store. May I suggest you park in the northwest corner of the Doubletree lot for a half hour on a Saturday or Sunday afternoon. Bicycle, car, pedestrian interactions can be scary at times. I’ve attached a copy of my letter to the editor in case you didn’t see it. Can the letter be attached to the public record of the meeting? As always, thanks. Alex IF NOT NOW, WHEN? One of the items on Thursday, April 25th Council agenda was whether or not to proceed with the last remaining project from the voter approved Walkability Bond. It is a tunnel under Kearns Boulevard connecting the Snow Creek path to the Yarrow/Doubletree. The WALC list of projects was the result of a study to create improved walkability and connectivity. The item was up for public comment. Three of us attended to offer our support to proceed. The three council members in attendance each voiced their opinions and reasoning behind not moving forward. The first comment was that many changes have occurred in Park City over the past 16 years. The project has reached a total cost of $18.6 million. What was not considered is the City's out of pocket was about $6.8 million. The balance of $11.8 million is to be paid by UDOT, the Sewer District, the county Transportation Fund and the balance of the WALC bond. It's likely that funding will go away if not used. That's akin to someone offering to sell you their $18 million house for $7 million and saying no thanks. Next was a discussion of a short term solution to add a cross walk with a pedestrian island near the intersection of Snow Creek Drive and Kearns. The city's own Transit Engineer said he could not support that, citing safety reasons. Among the those would have people waiting in the middle of the road competing with traffic making left turns into Snow Creek to get to the Park City Market shopping center. It was observed that if cars had to wait a little bit that would be ok. We could also wait until the Doubletree/Yarrow application is approved but who knows how long that approval could take and if will even be built. Another option suggested considering moving the tunnel farther east (away from Park Ave). This could work but is it the best option? A tunnel in the proposed location provides the best location providing Old Town residents the ability to ride/walk from Old Town to Snow Creek to Kimball Junction without having to cross a major road. That's significant! No one can argue that our system of tunnels has provided us with safe routes to walk and ride: Comstock, the High School, Bonanza Deer, Valley Drive and several more into Old Town. We approved a $15m bond in 2008 to improve walkability and connectivity. It's true that many things that have changed over the ensuing years but those two objectives remain. This tunnel is another integral part of meeting those objectives. Council should reconsider their direction to staff and allow the two absent members to voice their opinions. At a minimum it should be accounted for in the Capital Improvement budget so the money is there if the project moves forward. What's the answer to the question "if not now, when?" It his highly unlikely this tunnel will ever happen if not now.
source: eComment (written; published verbatim in council meeting minutes)

comment: I would like to provide comment on the proposed amendment to the e-bike pilot program that is being considered today, 6/28. I very strongly oppose the amendment as written. I support the council’s consideration of expanding the program, but this needs to be far more thought through, with ample input from the community and Mountain Trails Foundation. Thank you for voting no on this amendment.

comment: I would characterize this week’s agenda item, SR-248 study, as an outdated corridor study to engineer a solution in order to expedite federal grant monies as a string without a beginning or an end, and all for a cool million dollars. Viability isn’t a solution on its own. I recommend you skip tasks 1-3 and start with task 4 with a highly qualified town planner in order to ensure transportation mode changes actually benefit EVERYONE year round.
